A savings plan deposits \$300 at the START of each year for 10 years at 5%. Accumulated value at end of year 10?
The present value of an $n$-year annuity-immediate of 1 is 8.5 at rate $i$, and $v^n = 0.49$. Find $i$.
questions.explain: $a_{\overline{n}|} = (1 - v^n)/i \Rightarrow 8.5 = (1 - 0.49)/i = 0.51/i \Rightarrow i = 0.06 = 6\%$.

concepts.title: Perpetuities & Varying Annuities
concepts.tagline: Payments forever, or payments that grow. The shortcuts here turn intimidating streams into one-line answers.

sections.body: Now the payments stop being polite. Some streams run *forever* (perpetuities — endowments, consols, dividend-paying stocks); some *climb* every year (increasing annuities — pensions with cost-of-living bumps). They look like infinite sums you could never add by hand, and that's exactly the point: each collapses to a one-line closed form, and the exam pays you handsomely for recognizing the pattern on sight. The secret is that every one of these is *still* a geometric series — you already own the machinery.

sections.title: Why 'forever' costs a finite, small amount
sections.body:
It feels paradoxical that paying \$1 every year *for eternity* has a finite price — but discounting is relentless. The payment in year 50 is worth $v^{50}$; in year 100, $v^{100}$ — vanishingly small. The far tail of the stream contributes almost nothing, so the infinite sum *converges*. Concretely, at 5% a perpetuity of \$1 forever is worth just $1/0.05 = \$20$ today. Twenty dollars buys an infinite stream, because by year 100 each dollar is worth less than a penny in today's money.

Increasing streams add a second moving part — the payment size grows while the discount shrinks it — and the closed forms simply bookkeep that tug-of-war between growth and discounting.

sections.title: Deriving the perpetuity from the annuity limit
sections.body:
Don't memorize $1/i$ — *take a limit.* A perpetuity-immediate is an annuity-immediate with $n \to \infty$: $$\frac{1}{i}\text{-perpetuity} = \lim_{n\to\infty} a_{\overline{n}|} = \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1 - v^n}{i}.$$ Since $|v| < 1$, $v^n \to 0$ as $n\to\infty$, leaving $$a_{\overline{\infty}|} = \frac{1 - 0}{i} = \frac{1}{i}.$$ Clean. The perpetuity-**due** lands one period earlier, so multiply by $(1+i)$: $\frac{1+i}{i} = \frac{1}{d}$.

**Increasing perpetuity** (payments $1, 2, 3, \dots$ forever): here's the slick derivation. Think of it as *layers* of level perpetuities. A \$1 perpetuity starting year 1 is worth $1/i$. Another \$1 perpetuity starting year 2 (worth $\frac{1}{i}\cdot v$ today) stacks on top. Another starting year 3, and so on. Summing those layers, $\frac{1}{i}(1 + v + v^2 + \cdots) = \frac{1}{i}\cdot\frac{1}{1-v} = \frac{1}{i}\cdot\frac{1}{iv} = \frac{1}{i^2}\cdot\frac{1}{v}$... cleaner to state the standard result: $$(I a)_{\overline{\infty}|} = \frac{1}{i} + \frac{1}{i^2} = \frac{i+1}{i^2}.$$ For the *finite* increasing annuity, $(Ia)_{\overline{n}|} = \dfrac{\ddot{a}_{\overline{n}|} - n v^n}{i}$.

sections.title: The geometrically-growing perpetuity — derive 1/(i−g)
sections.body: This one is a dividend-model workhorse, so derive it once and own it. Payments grow by a factor $(1+g)$ each year: first payment 1 at year 1, then $(1+g)$, then $(1+g)^2$, .... Present value: $$PV = v + (1+g)v^2 + (1+g)^2 v^3 + \cdots$$ Factor out $v$: $PV = v\left[1 + (1+g)v + ((1+g)v)^2 + \cdots\right]$ — a geometric series with ratio $r = (1+g)v$. It sums (when $r<1$, i.e. $g<i$) to $\frac{1}{1-r}$: $$PV = \frac{v}{1 - (1+g)v}.$$ Multiply top and bottom by $(1+i)$ (recall $v=\frac{1}{1+i}$): $$PV = \frac{1}{(1+i) - (1+g)} = \frac{1}{i - g}.$$ So the famous $\frac{1}{i-g}$ isn't a separate fact — it's the geometric-series sum in disguise. Valid only when $i > g$; if growth outran the discount rate the sum would diverge.

sections.title: Worked example — a growing-dividend valuation
sections.body: A perpetuity pays \$100 at the end of year 1, \$200 at year 2, \$300 at year 3, and so on forever (arithmetic growth). At $i = 10\%$, find its present value.
steps: **Recognize the shape:** payments $100, 200, 300, \dots$ are $100\times(1, 2, 3, \dots)$ — that's 100 copies of an increasing perpetuity-immediate with base 1.
**Apply the derived increasing-perpetuity formula:** per unit, $\dfrac{1}{i} + \dfrac{1}{i^2} = \dfrac{1}{0.1} + \dfrac{1}{0.01} = 10 + 100 = 110$.
**Don't confuse arithmetic with geometric growth:** payments $+\$100$ each year is *arithmetic* (use $Ia$); payments $\times 1.10$ each year would be *geometric* (use $1/(i-g)$).

sections.title: Split any messy stream into level + increasing layers
sections.body: A stream like "\$500 in year 1, then rising \$100 a year" looks custom, but it's two familiar pieces glued together: a **level** annuity of \$400 forever-or-$n$-years, *plus* an **increasing** annuity $(Ia)$ with base \$100 (giving $400+100=500$ in year 1, $400+200=600$ in year 2, ...). Price each layer with its own closed form and add. This decompose-and-add move cracks the large majority of varying-annuity questions — whenever a stream resists one formula, look for the level part hiding inside it.

sections.title: Immediate vs due, and arithmetic vs geometric growth
sections.body: Two traps live here. **(1) Perpetuity timing:** immediate is $1/i$, due is $1/d$ — pick wrong and you drop a $(1+i)$. **(2) Growth type:** "increases by \$50 each year" is *arithmetic* → use $(Ia)$ / the $1/i+1/i^2$ family; "increases by 5% each year" is *geometric* → use $1/(i-g)$. They are completely different formulas, and the words 'by \$X' versus 'by X%' are your only clue. Read that phrase twice before choosing. And for $1/(i-g)$, sanity-check $i>g$ — otherwise the stream has no finite value.

cards.front: Why does a perpetuity's value $1/i$ fall out of the annuity formula?
cards.back: It's $\lim_{n\to\infty} a_{\overline{n}|} = \lim (1-v^n)/i$; since $v^n\to 0$, it collapses to $1/i$. The infinite tail is discounted to nothing.

cards.front: Where does the dividend-model $1/(i-g)$ come from?
cards.back: It's the sum of the geometric series $v + (1+g)v^2 + \cdots$ with ratio $(1+g)v$; summing and simplifying gives $1/(i-g)$, valid for $i>g$.

questions.q: A perpetuity pays \$50 at the end of each year forever. At 5% effective, find its present value.
questions.explain: Perpetuity-immediate: $50/0.05 = 1000$.

questions.q: A perpetuity-due pays \$100 per year at 8%. Find its present value.
A stock pays \$4 next year, growing 3% annually forever. At a 9% discount rate, find the price.
An increasing perpetuity pays \$10, \$20, \$30, ... at year-ends forever, at 5%. Find its present value.

concepts.title: Deferred & Continuous Annuities
concepts.tagline: Push a level annuity into the future with one discount factor, or let the payments flow continuously and integrate. Two variations the exam tests cleanly.

sections.body: Two natural twists on the level annuity, and both are *less* work than they look. A **deferred** annuity simply doesn't start paying for a while — a pension that kicks in at retirement, a loan with a grace period. A **continuous** annuity pays in an unbroken trickle instead of discrete lumps — the idealized limit of paying weekly, then daily, then every instant. Here's the reassuring truth: neither is a new formula to memorize. Each is the *level annuity you already own*, multiplied by exactly one extra factor. Learn which factor, and why, and these become free points.

sections.title: Defer = value at its own start, then slide it back
sections.body:
A deferred annuity isn't a different creature — it's an ordinary annuity that you're looking at *early*. So value it the lazy way: pretend it starts now, price it with the plain formula, then **drag that single lump sum back** across the deferral gap with one discount factor $v^m$. The annuity doesn't care from which date you observe it; you value it where it naturally lives (one period before its first payment) and then discount that value to today.

The **continuous** annuity comes from a different limit. Pay \$1/year as 12 monthly bits, then 365 daily bits, then infinitely many infinitesimal bits — the discrete sum $\sum v^t$ smooths into the integral $\int_0^n v^t\,dt$. Integration is just summation taken to the continuous limit, and it produces a tidy closed form.

sections.title: Deriving the continuous annuity by integration
sections.body:
**Deferred** first (the easy one). An $m$-year deferred, $n$-payment annuity-immediate is value-then-discount: $$_{m|}a_{\overline{n}|} = v^m\, a_{\overline{n}|}.$$ There's also a slick subtraction identity — a full $(m+n)$-year annuity minus the first $m$ years you don't actually receive: $_{m|}a_{\overline{n}|} = a_{\overline{m+n}|} - a_{\overline{m}|}$. Same number, two viewpoints.

**Continuous**, derived from scratch. Sum (integrate) the discount factor over the payment window: $$\bar a_{\overline{n}|} = \int_0^n v^t\,dt.$$ Write $v^t = e^{t\ln v} = e^{-\delta t}$ (since $\ln v = -\ln(1+i) = -\delta$). The integral of $e^{-\delta t}$ is $-\frac{1}{\delta}e^{-\delta t}$, so $$\bar a_{\overline{n}|} = \left[-\frac{e^{-\delta t}}{\delta}\right]_0^n = \frac{1 - e^{-\delta n}}{\delta} = \frac{1 - v^n}{\delta}.$$ Notice the result is the *spitting image* of $a_{\overline{n}|} = \frac{1-v^n}{i}$ — only the denominator changed from $i$ to the **force** $\delta$. The continuous analogue of the period rate is the instantaneous rate. Accumulated version: $\bar s_{\overline{n}|} = \frac{(1+i)^n - 1}{\delta}$.

sections.title: Worked example 1 — a deferred annuity
sections.body: An annuity pays \$1000 at the end of each year for 10 years, but the first payment is at the end of year 6 (a 5-year deferral). At $i = 7\%$, find the present value. Use $a_{\overline{10}|} = 7.0236$.
steps: **Where does the plain formula plant the value?** $a_{\overline{10}|}$ values the stream one period before its first payment. First payment is at $t=6$, so the formula's value sits at $t=5$.
**Value it there:** $1000\,a_{\overline{10}|} = 1000(7.0236) = 7023.60$, a lump sum located at $t=5$.
**Result:** $PV = 7023.60 \times 0.71299 = \$5008.7$. (The deferral exponent is 5, not 6 — that off-by-one is the whole game.)

sections.title: Worked example 2 — continuous annuity, then the i/δ shortcut
sections.body: A continuous annuity pays at rate \$1/year for 5 years at $i = 7\%$ effective ($\delta = \ln 1.07 = 0.06766$). Find $\bar a_{\overline{5}|}$ directly, then show it equals $\frac{i}{\delta}a_{\overline{5}|}$.
steps: **Why slightly bigger than discrete?** A continuous stream delivers money a touch *earlier* within each year, so its PV exceeds the year-end annuity by exactly the factor $i/\delta > 1$.

sections.title: Two reusable conversion factors
sections.body: Don't re-derive — convert. (1) **Continuous from discrete:** $\bar a_{\overline{n}|} = \frac{i}{\delta}\,a_{\overline{n}|}$. Already have the discrete annuity factor? One multiply by $i/\delta$ and you're done — no integral needed. Because $i > \delta$, expect a slightly larger number. (2) **Deferred from plain:** value the annuity at its natural start, then multiply by $v^{(\text{deferral})}$. Both moves reduce a scary-looking variant to your level-annuity home base plus a single factor.

sections.title: The deferral exponent is one less than you think
sections.body: The signature deferred-annuity mistake is an off-by-one on the discount power. The annuity-immediate formula *already* values the stream **one period before the first payment** — that's baked in. So if the first payment is at time $m+1$, the formula's value sits at time $m$, and you discount by $v^{m}$, **not** $v^{m+1}$. Equivalently: count the number of *empty* periods before the formula's valuation point, not before the first payment. Always sketch the timeline, mark where the plain formula 'plants its flag,' and count the gap from there to today.

cards.front: Where does the continuous annuity formula $\frac{1-v^n}{\delta}$ come from?
cards.back: From $\int_0^n v^t dt = \int_0^n e^{-\delta t}dt = \frac{1-e^{-\delta n}}{\delta} = \frac{1-v^n}{\delta}$. It mirrors the discrete $\frac{1-v^n}{i}$ with $i$ replaced by the force $\delta$.

cards.front: First payment of a deferred annuity is at time $m+1$ — what's the discount exponent, and why?
cards.back: $v^m$. The immediate formula already values the stream at time $m$ (one period before the first payment), so you only discount $m$ more periods to today.

questions.q: A 4-year annuity-immediate of \$1 is deferred 3 years ($a_{\overline{4}|}=3.3872$ at 7%, $v^3=0.8163$). Find its present value.
A continuous annuity pays at rate \$1/year for 5 years. If $\delta=0.06$ and $v^5=0.7408$, find $\bar a_{\overline{5}|}$.
Given $a_{\overline{n}|}=8.0$, $i=0.06$, $\delta=0.0583$, find the continuous annuity $\bar a_{\overline{n}|}$.
An annuity's first of 10 annual payments occurs at $t=6$. By what factor do you discount the standard $a_{\overline{10}|}$ value?
questions.explain: The immediate formula values the annuity at $t=5$ (one period before the first payment at $t=6$), so discount by $v^5$.

questions.q: Why is a continuous annuity worth more than the otherwise-identical annuity-immediate?
choices: It is not — they are equal
questions.explain: A continuous stream effectively delivers money earlier within each period, so its PV is larger by the factor $i/\delta>1$.

concepts.title: Geometric (Growing) Annuities
concepts.tagline: Payments that grow by a fixed percentage each year — pensions with COLA, dividends. One adjusted-rate trick turns them back into a level annuity.

sections.body: Real money rarely stays flat. Salaries get cost-of-living raises, dividends grow, rents step up a fixed percentage every year. A **geometric annuity** is a stream where each payment is a constant *multiple* $(1+g)$ of the one before. It looks like a brand-new beast — but one clever change of rate collapses it right back into the level annuity you already know cold. The whole concept is a single trick: *fold the growth into the discount rate.*

sections.title: Growth and discounting are tug-of-war on the same rope
sections.body: Each year two things happen to a future payment. It *grows* by $(1+g)$ (good for you), and it gets *discounted* by another $(1+i)$ (shrinks its present value). Those two factors are fighting over the same payment, and what actually matters is the **net** of the two. So define a single **adjusted rate** $j$ that captures the net effect: $$1 + j = \frac{1+i}{1+g}.$$ Read it literally — you discount at $(1+i)$ but get $(1+g)$ of growth back, so the *effective* shrink-per-year is the ratio. Once you've defined $j$, a *growing* annuity at rate $i$ becomes a plain *level* annuity at rate $j$ (with a small rescaling). The intimidating topic reduces to: compute $j$, then use $a_{\overline{n}|}$ at $j$.

sections.title: Deriving the growing-annuity formula
sections.body: First payment \$1 at $t=1$, then growing by $(1+g)$ each year for $n$ payments, discounted at $i$. Write out the present value: $$PV = \frac{1}{1+i} + \frac{1+g}{(1+i)^2} + \cdots + \frac{(1+g)^{n-1}}{(1+i)^n}.$$ Factor $\frac{1}{1+i}$ from every term: $PV = \frac{1}{1+i}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\left(\frac{1+g}{1+i}\right)^k$ — a geometric series with ratio $r = \frac{1+g}{1+i} = \frac{1}{1+j}$. Summing $\frac{1-r^n}{1-r}$ and simplifying (use $1 - r = 1 - \frac{1+g}{1+i} = \frac{i-g}{1+i}$) gives the clean closed form: $$PV = \frac{1 - \left(\frac{1+g}{1+i}\right)^n}{i - g}.$$ Let $n\to\infty$: if $i>g$ the ratio $r<1$ so $r^n\to 0$, leaving the famous **growing perpetuity** $$PV = \frac{1}{i-g}.$$ Equivalent calculator-friendly recipe: compute the level annuity $a_{\overline{n}|}$ at the adjusted rate $j$, then divide by $(1+g)$ — same answer, fewer keystrokes.

sections.title: Worked example 1 — a growing perpetuity (Gordon growth)
sections.body: A perpetuity pays \$100 at the end of year 1, growing 3% per year forever, discounted at 8%. Find its present value.
steps: **Identify it's geometric and infinite:** payments $\times 1.03$ each year, forever → growing-perpetuity formula.
**Sanity check against the level case:** a *flat* \$100 perpetuity at 8% is $100/0.08 = \$1250$; the 3% growth lifts it to \$2000. Growth makes it worth more — as it must.

sections.title: Worked example 2 — the adjusted-rate trick on a finite annuity
sections.body: A 20-year annuity pays \$1000 at the end of year 1, increasing 4% each year, discounted at 9%. Price it using the adjusted-rate method to show the trick in action.
steps: **Cross-check with the direct formula:** $\dfrac{1 - (1.04/1.09)^{20}}{0.09-0.04} = \dfrac{1 - 0.39157}{0.05} = \dfrac{0.60843}{0.05}\times\frac{1}{1.04}\cdots$ — same \$12{,}167. The trick and the formula are one and the same.

sections.title: Memorize Gordon growth; derive the rest from j
sections.body: Burn $\dfrac{P_1}{i-g}$ into memory — the **Gordon growth model** of finance — because dividend and pension questions hand it to you constantly, and it's a one-liner. For *finite* growing annuities, don't memorize the bulky formula; instead compute the adjusted rate $1+j=\frac{1+i}{1+g}$, treat the stream as a plain level annuity at $j$, and divide by $(1+g)$ at the end. One reusable move handles every geometric annuity the exam can throw at you.

sections.title: First payment, $i>g$, and percent-vs-dollar growth
sections.body: Three landmines. **(1)** In $\frac{P_1}{i-g}$, the numerator is the payment at $t=1$ — *not* a 'base' figure quoted before the first raise, and not a $t=0$ amount. Read the timeline. **(2)** The perpetuity needs $i>g$; if $g\ge i$ payments grow at least as fast as you discount and the value is infinite — the shortcut is meaningless (a finite growing *annuity* still works via the general formula). **(3)** Don't confuse this with arithmetic growth: "increases 4% a year" is geometric (this concept); "increases by \$40 a year" is arithmetic (use $Ia$). The single word percent-vs-dollars decides which formula you reach for.

cards.front: What single substitution turns a growing annuity into a level one, and why?
cards.back: The adjusted rate $1+j = \frac{1+i}{1+g}$ — it nets growth against discounting. Then value at $j$ as a level annuity and divide by $(1+g)$.

cards.front: Derive the growing-perpetuity value and state its condition.
cards.back: The PV is the geometric series $\frac{1}{1+i}\sum (\frac{1+g}{1+i})^k$; for $i>g$ the ratio <1 and it sums to $\frac{1}{i-g}$ (Gordon growth). If $g\ge i$ it diverges.

questions.q: A perpetuity pays \$200 in year 1, growing 4% yearly, discounted at 9%. Find its present value.
A dividend of \$5 next year grows 6% forever; the discount rate is 11%. Find the present value.
For a growing perpetuity, what condition must hold for a finite present value?
questions.explain: The series $\sum \frac{(1+g)^{t-1}}{(1+i)^t}$ converges only when $i>g$.

questions.q: A 3-payment annuity pays \$100, then grows 10% each year, discounted at 10%. Find the present value.
questions.explain: When $g=i$, each discounted payment equals $\frac{100}{1.1}=90.91$, and there are 3 of them: $3\times90.91=272.73$.

questions.q: The growing-perpetuity formula $\frac{P_1}{i-g}$ is also known in finance as the:
questions.explain: It is the Gordon growth (dividend discount) model.

modules.title: Loans
modules.blurb: Amortization and the split of each payment into interest and principal. Outstanding balance two ways — prospective and retrospective — and the sinking-fund alternative.

concepts.title: Loan Amortization
concepts.tagline: Every payment is part interest, part principal. The outstanding balance is just the present value of what is left to pay.

sections.body: Amortization questions are free points once one sentence lives in your bones: **the outstanding balance is the present value of the payments you still owe.** Not a schedule to grind through, not a balance to track row by row — just a present value of what remains. From that single anchor, every quantity the exam asks for (this month's interest, this month's principal, the balance after payment 17) falls out in two lines. We'll derive *why* each payment splits the way it does so you never have to memorize the split.

sections.title: Why early payments are almost all interest
sections.body: Each level payment $R$ does two jobs: first it pays the interest that just accrued on the balance, and whatever is left chips away at the principal. Early in the loan the balance is *huge*, so the interest it throws off is huge, and only a sliver of your payment touches principal. As principal slowly falls, the interest it generates falls too — so more of each fixed payment attacks principal, and the payoff accelerates. That's why your first mortgage payments feel like they barely move the balance: the principal-repayment curve is **back-loaded**, small at first and snowballing later. Crucially, the principal portions themselves grow by exactly $(1+i)$ each period — a fact we'll prove, and one the exam loves to test.

sections.title: Deriving the balance, interest, and principal split
sections.body:
**Balance (prospective).** The lender is owed exactly the present value of the remaining payments. After $t$ payments, $n-t$ payments of $R$ remain, so $$B_t = R\,a_{\overline{n-t}|}.$$ That's the master equation of value applied to 'what's left' — nothing new.

**Interest in the next payment.** Interest accrues on the current balance for one period: $$I_{t+1} = i\,B_t.$$

**Principal in the next payment.** Whatever the payment doesn't spend on interest: $$P_{t+1} = R - I_{t+1} = R - i\,B_t.$$

**Why principal grows by $(1+i)$.** Here's the proof. $P_{t+1} = R - iB_t$ and $P_t = R - iB_{t-1}$. Subtract: $P_{t+1} - P_t = -i(B_t - B_{t-1}) = -i(-P_t) = iP_t$ (since the balance drops by exactly the principal paid). So $P_{t+1} = P_t + iP_t = (1+i)P_t$. Each principal repayment is the previous one grown by $(1+i)$ — a geometric ladder. Combined with $P_1 = R - iB_0 = R(1 - v^n)$, you can jump to *any* principal portion: $P_{t+1} = R\,v^{\,n-t}$.

sections.title: Worked example 1 — split a payment into interest and principal
sections.body: A \$10{,}000 loan at 8% is repaid with level annual payments over 5 years. Find the payment, then the interest and principal in payment 1.
steps: **Payment from the loan-as-annuity equation:** $10{,}000 = R\,a_{\overline{5}|}$ with $a_{\overline{5}|} = 3.9927$, so $R = 10{,}000/3.9927 = \$2504.56$.
**Interest in payment 1:** interest on the full starting balance, $I_1 = 0.08 \times 10{,}000 = \$800$.

sections.title: Worked example 2 — balance after several payments, two ways
sections.body: For the same \$10{,}000 / 8% / 5-year loan ($R = 2504.56$), find the outstanding balance just after payment 3, using both the prospective and retrospective methods to show they agree.
steps: **Retrospective (accumulate the loan, subtract accumulated payments):** $B_3 = 10{,}000(1.08)^3 - R\,s_{\overline{3}|} = 12{,}597.1 - 2504.56(3.2464) = 12{,}597.1 - 8130.8 = \$4466.3$.
**They match** (to rounding). Use whichever side has fewer terms — here prospective wins with only 2 payments left versus 3 behind.

sections.title: Prospective balance, then i×balance — the two-line solve
sections.body: Almost every amortization question yields to one reflex: get the balance as the PV of what's left, $B_t = R\,a_{\overline{n-t}|}$, then the very next interest is $i\times B_t$ and the principal is the remainder $R - iB_t$. No row-by-row schedule, no accumulation grind. A companion shortcut for principal: since the portions form a geometric ladder, the principal in payment $t+1$ is $P_{t+1} = R\,v^{\,n-t}$ — letting you snipe a single year's principal without computing any balance at all.

sections.title: Prospective vs retrospective — and changed payments
sections.body: The **prospective** balance (PV of future payments) and the **retrospective** balance (accumulated loan minus accumulated payments) must always agree — they're the same equation of value seen from opposite ends. But the shortcut $B_t = R\,a_{\overline{n-t}|}$ secretly assumes the payment $R$ and rate $i$ stay constant for the *whole* remaining term. The moment a loan has an irregular final payment, a payment holiday, or a rate change, that clean formula lies — you must rebuild from the actual remaining schedule. When a problem says 'the last payment is adjusted to exactly retire the loan,' that's your cue the simple formula no longer applies to the tail.

cards.front: Why does the outstanding balance equal $R\,a_{\overline{n-t}|}$?
cards.back: Because the lender is owed precisely the present value of the payments still to come — it's the equation of value applied to the remaining $n-t$ payments.

cards.front: Prove that successive principal repayments grow by $(1+i)$.
cards.back: $P_{t+1}-P_t = -i(B_t-B_{t-1}) = -i(-P_t) = iP_t$, so $P_{t+1}=(1+i)P_t$. The principal portions form a geometric ladder; equivalently $P_{t+1}=R\,v^{n-t}$.

questions.q: A \$20,000 loan at 6% is repaid with level annual payments over 10 years. Find the annual payment. ($a_{\overline{10}|} = 7.3601$)
For that same loan, how much interest is in the first payment?
A loan has level payments of \$500 with 6 payments remaining at 7%. What is the outstanding balance now? ($a_{\overline{6}|} = 4.7665$)
questions.explain: Prospective: $B = 500 \times a_{\overline{6}|} = 500(4.7665) = 2383$.

questions.q: If the principal repaid in the first payment of a 5-year loan is \$1704.56 at 8%, what is the principal repaid in the second payment?
questions.explain: Principal repayments grow by $(1+i)$: $1704.56 \times 1.08 = 1840.92$.

questions.q: A loan is repaid with 12 level payments. The interest in payment 1 is \$600 and the payment is \$1000. What is the original loan amount if $i = 6\%$?
questions.explain: $I_1 = i \times L \Rightarrow 600 = 0.06 L \Rightarrow L = 10000$.

concepts.title: The Sinking-Fund Method
concepts.tagline: Pay the lender only interest, and grow the principal separately in a side account. Two interest rates, one clean comparison to amortization.

sections.body: There are two philosophies for killing a loan. **Amortization** blends interest and principal into every payment, whittling the balance to zero. The **sinking-fund method** splits those jobs apart: you pay the lender *interest only* each period — the principal never moves — while quietly feeding a separate side account that grows on its own until, at maturity, it has swollen to exactly the loan amount and extinguishes it in one lump. The exam adores pitting the two against each other, because the comparison turns on a subtle point: the fund usually earns a *different* rate than the loan charges.

sections.title: Interest goes out; savings grow on the side
sections.body: Two money streams run in parallel and you must not let them touch. **Stream one:** you owe the lender interest on the *whole* loan, every single period, $Li$ — and because you never repay principal until the end, that interest charge never shrinks. **Stream two:** you make level deposits $D$ into your own sinking fund, which compounds at *its* rate $j$ (usually lower than the loan rate $i$, because a safe savings vehicle pays less than what you're charged to borrow). The fund climbs until its balance hits $L$, at which instant you hand it to the lender and the debt vanishes. Your true periodic cost is the sum of the two streams: constant interest plus the level deposit.

sections.title: Building the two-stream payment
sections.body: Loan $L$, lender's rate $i$, sinking-fund rate $j$, term $n$. **Interest stream:** principal stays at $L$, so each period you pay $Li$ — flat, forever, until maturity. **Deposit stream:** the deposit $D$ must accumulate to the full loan by time $n$. Since $n$ level deposits at rate $j$ grow to $D\,s_{\overline{n}|j}$, set that equal to $L$ and solve: $$D\,s_{\overline{n}|j} = L \;\Rightarrow\; D = \frac{L}{s_{\overline{n}|j}}.$$ **Total periodic outlay:** $$R = Li + \frac{L}{s_{\overline{n}|j}}.$$ Beautiful fact worth proving to yourself: when the two rates coincide, $i = j$, this *exactly* reproduces the amortization payment $L/a_{\overline{n}|}$. The reason is the identity $\frac{1}{a_{\overline{n}|}} = \frac{1}{s_{\overline{n}|}} + i$ — the level-annuity payment is secretly 'interest plus a sinking-fund deposit' all along. So amortization is just the sinking-fund method with the fund earning the loan rate.

sections.title: Worked example 1 — total payment with two rates
sections.body: A \$10{,}000 loan runs 5 years. The lender charges 8%; your sinking fund earns only 6%. Given $s_{\overline{5}|6\%} = 5.6371$, find the total annual payment, and compare to straight amortization.
steps: **Interest stream:** $10{,}000 \times 0.08 = \$800$ to the lender every year (never changes).

**Compare to amortization at 8%:** $10{,}000/a_{\overline{5}|8\%} = 10{,}000/3.9927 = \$2504.6$ — *cheaper.* The sinking fund costs more here precisely because the fund (6%) earns less than the loan rate (8%); the rate gap is the borrower's penalty.

sections.title: Worked example 2 — net interest in a given year
sections.body: A favorite exam twist: the borrower's *net* cost isn't just $Li$, because the sinking fund is itself earning interest. For the same loan ($D = 1773.96$, $j = 6\%$), find the net interest cost in year 3.
steps: **Fund balance at the start of year 3** (just after the 2nd deposit) $= D\,s_{\overline{2}|6\%} = 1773.96 \times 2.06 = \$3654.4$.
**Interest the fund earns in year 3:** $0.06 \times 3654.4 = \$219.3$ — this offsets your cost.
**Gross interest to the lender:** $Li = \$800$ as always.

**Net interest cost in year 3:** $800 - 219.3 = \$580.7$. As the fund grows, the interest it throws off rises, so your net cost falls year over year — mirroring how amortization's interest portion declines.

sections.title: Net cost = gross interest minus fund earnings
sections.body: To track the 'real' cost in any year, don't just quote $Li$ — subtract what the fund earned: net interest $= Li - j\,(\text{fund balance})$, where the fund balance at time $t$ is $D\,s_{\overline{t}|j}$. This mirrors amortization's shrinking interest column, and it's the lens that makes the $i=j$ equivalence obvious: when the fund earns the loan rate, the net cost schedule *is* the amortization schedule. Memorize the bridge identity $\frac{1}{a_{\overline{n}|}} = \frac{1}{s_{\overline{n}|}} + i$ — it converts between the two worlds in one line.

sections.title: Two rates, and a principal that never moves
sections.body: The whole concept hinges on keeping **two rates** straight: $i$ is charged by the lender (drives the interest payment $Li$), while $j$ is earned by you (drives the accumulation $s_{\overline{n}|j}$). Swap them — put the loan rate inside the $s$ factor, or accumulate at the loan rate — and the answer collapses. Second trap: the outstanding *principal* under a sinking fund does **not** amortize down; it sits at $L$ the entire term, so the interest payment is a flat $Li$ every period, never declining. (What declines is the *net* cost, via fund earnings — a different quantity.)

cards.front: Why does the sinking-fund total equal the amortization payment when $i=j$?
cards.back: Because of the identity $\frac{1}{a_{\overline{n}|}} = \frac{1}{s_{\overline{n}|}} + i$: the amortization payment $L/a_{\overline{n}|}$ is literally interest $Li$ plus a sinking-fund deposit $L/s_{\overline{n}|}$ when both use the same rate.

cards.front: Under a sinking fund, what stays constant and what changes year to year?
cards.back: The principal ($L$) and gross interest to the lender ($Li$) stay flat the whole term; the fund balance grows, so the *net* interest cost $Li - j(\text{fund balance})$ falls each year.

questions.q: A \$5000 loan at 10% uses a sinking fund earning 8%, 4 years, $s_{\overline{4}|8\%}=4.5061$. Find the annual sinking-fund deposit.
Same loan: \$5000 at 10% lender rate. What is the annual interest paid to the lender?
questions.explain: Interest only on the full principal: $5000(0.10)=500$, every year.

questions.q: Combine the two: total annual payment for the \$5000 loan (interest \$500, deposit \$1109.61)?
Under the sinking-fund method, the outstanding loan principal over time:
questions.explain: Only interest is paid to the lender; principal is retired in a lump at maturity, so it stays at $L$ throughout.

questions.q: The sinking-fund total payment equals the amortization payment exactly when:
questions.explain: With equal rates, $Li + L/s_{\overline{n}|} = L/a_{\overline{n}|}$, reproducing amortization.

modules.title: Bonds
modules.blurb: Pricing coupon bonds, the premium/discount relationship to the yield, and book value via amortization of the bond's premium or discount.

concepts.title: Bond Pricing & Premium/Discount
concepts.tagline: A bond is an annuity of coupons plus a lump-sum redemption. Whether it trades above or below par is decided by one comparison.

sections.body: Bonds look like a new topic but they are just an annuity (the coupons) plus a single future payment (the redemption). Price both with tools you already have. The one new insight — premium vs discount — is a 10-second comparison that the exam tests constantly.

sections.title: Coupon rate vs yield decides premium or discount
sections.body: If a bond's **coupon rate beats the market yield**, investors will pay *extra* for that generous coupon — it trades at a **premium** (price above redemption). If the coupon lags the yield, nobody pays full price, so it trades at a **discount**. Coupon equals yield → it trades exactly at par. That comparison alone tells you the direction before any arithmetic.

sections.title: The price formula
sections.body: $$P = F r\,a_{\overline{n}|} + C v^n$$ where $F$ is face value, $r$ the coupon rate per period, $Fr$ the coupon payment, $C$ the redemption value, $n$ the number of coupons, and $i$ (inside $a$ and $v$) the yield per period. Premium $= P - C$ when positive; discount $= C - P$ when $P < C$.

sections.title: Price a 10-year coupon bond
sections.body: A \$1000 par bond pays 8% annual coupons, redeems at par in 10 years, and is priced to yield 6%. Find the price.
steps: Coupon rate 8% exceeds yield 6%, so the bond trades at a premium — confirmed, $P > 1000$.

sections.title: Predict premium/discount before computing
sections.body: Glance at coupon vs yield first. Coupon > yield → premium → answer must exceed redemption. Coupon < yield → discount → below redemption. This instantly eliminates wrong answer choices and catches keystroke errors: if you predicted premium but computed a price below par, you mis-keyed something.

sections.title: Mismatched coupon and yield periods
sections.body: Most bonds pay **semiannual** coupons. Then $n$ is the number of *half-years*, the coupon is $Fr/2$ per period, and the yield must be the *semiannual* yield ($i^{(2)}/2$). Plugging an annual yield with a semiannual coupon count is the signature bond-pricing mistake — halve and double consistently.

cards.front: Bond price formula?
cards.back: $P = Fr\,a_{\overline{n}|} + Cv^n$ — coupons as an annuity plus discounted redemption.

cards.front: When does a bond trade at a premium?
cards.back: When the coupon rate exceeds the yield rate, so $P > C$.

cards.front: Semiannual bond: what gets halved and doubled?
cards.back: Coupon is $Fr/2$ per period, yield is per half-year, and $n$ counts half-years (double the years).

questions.q: A \$1000 par bond with 5% annual coupons redeems at par in 8 years, priced to yield 5%. Its price is:
questions.explain: Coupon rate equals yield (5% = 5%), so the bond is priced exactly at par: \$1000.

questions.q: A bond with a coupon rate below its yield rate will be priced:
questions.explain: Coupon < yield means the coupons are unattractive, so the price falls below redemption — a discount bond.

questions.q: A \$1000 par, 6% annual-coupon bond redeems at par in 5 years, yielding 8%. Find the price. ($a_{\overline{5}|}=3.9927$ at 8%, $v^5=0.68058$)
A \$1000 par bond pays 7% annual coupons, redeems at \$1050 in 10 years, and yields 7%. The price is:
questions.explain: Coupon is $1000(0.07)=70$ on a $1050$ redemption. The price $P = 70a_{\overline{10}|} + 1050v^{10}$ at 7% comes out between 1000 and 1050 because redemption exceeds face. (It equals about \$1025.)

questions.q: A semiannual bond has 6% annual coupons (paid twice yearly), \$1000 par, 3 years to maturity, yielding 8% annual convertible semiannually. How many periods and what coupon per period?
questions.explain: Semiannual: $n = 3\times2 = 6$ periods, coupon $= 1000(0.06)/2 = 30$ per period, yield $= 8\%/2 = 4\%$ per period.

concepts.title: Bond Amortization & Book Value
concepts.tagline: Between purchase and maturity a bond's book value glides to par. Each coupon splits into interest earned and a write-down (or write-up) of premium or discount.

sections.body: A bond bought at a premium is worth more than par today but redeems at par — so its book value must *fall* over time. Bought at a discount, it must *rise*. That glide is **amortization of premium** (or **accretion of discount**), and every coupon you receive quietly does double duty: part is true interest, part adjusts the book value toward par.

sections.title: The coupon is interest plus a correction
sections.body: Think of each period as earning the yield on what the bond is currently worth: interest $= i \times BV$. If the coupon you actually receive exceeds that earned interest (a premium bond, fat coupon), the surplus is a return *of* your overpayment — it writes the book value **down**. If the coupon falls short of earned interest (a discount bond), the shortfall is made up by the book value being written **up**. Either way the book value marches to par by maturity.

sections.title: Book value and the amortization split
sections.body: Book value at time $t$ = present value of remaining cash flows at the original yield $i$: $$BV_t = Fr\,a_{\overline{n-t}|i} + C\,v^{n-t}$$ Each coupon $Fr$ splits as: interest earned $= i\,BV_{t-1}$, and principal adjustment $= Fr - i\,BV_{t-1}$. **Premium** $= P - C$ amortizes down to 0; **discount** $= C - P$ accretes up to 0. The write-down/up amounts grow by $(1+i)$ each period.

widget.caption: Set the coupon rate against the yield and watch the book value glide to par: above-yield coupons make a **premium** bond amortize *downward*, below-yield coupons make a **discount** bond accrete *upward*. The write-down/write-up each period is exactly the gap between the coupon and the interest earned on the current book value.

sections.title: One line of the amortization schedule
sections.body: A \$1000 par bond with 8% annual coupons yields 6%, redeems at par. Its current book value is \$1075. Find this period's interest earned and premium amortized.
steps: New book value $= 1075 - 15.50 = 1059.50$ — closer to par, as a premium bond must be.

sections.title: Write-downs grow geometrically by $(1+i)$
sections.body: You rarely need the whole schedule. The principal-adjustment amounts form a geometric sequence: each period's write-down (or write-up) is $(1+i)$ times the previous one. So if the first premium amortized is $P_1$, the $k$-th is $P_1(1+i)^{k-1}$, and the total amortized over any stretch is a small geometric sum. This shortcuts most 'find the amortization in year $k$' questions.

sections.title: Interest is on book value, not par
sections.body: The earned interest each period is $i \times BV_{t-1}$ — the **yield** times the **current book value** — not the coupon, and not the yield times par. Students often compute interest on the face amount; that only coincides when the bond is at par. Second trap: amortization writes a premium *down* and a discount *up*; getting the sign backwards corrupts the entire schedule.

cards.front: Book value of a bond at time $t$?
cards.back: PV of remaining coupons and redemption at the original yield: $Fr\,a_{\overline{n-t}|}+Cv^{n-t}$.

cards.front: How does each coupon split?
cards.back: Interest earned $=i\,BV_{t-1}$; the rest adjusts (amortizes) the book value.

cards.front: Premium bond book value over time?
cards.back: Falls toward par (premium amortizes down).

cards.front: How do successive write-down amounts change?
cards.back: They grow by a factor of $(1+i)$ each period.

questions.q: A bond with book value \$980 yields 7% and pays a \$50 coupon. Find the interest earned this period.
Same bond (BV \$980, yield 7%, coupon \$50). Is it a discount or premium bond, and what is the book-value adjustment?
questions.explain: Coupon 50 < interest earned 68.60, so the shortfall \$18.60 writes the book value UP — a discount bond accreting toward par.

questions.q: A premium bond's first-year premium amortized is \$12 at yield 5%. What is the second-year amount?
questions.explain: Amortization grows by $(1+i)$: $12(1.05)=12.60$.

questions.q: If a bond is priced at par, the book-value amortization each period is:
questions.explain: At par the coupon exactly equals the interest earned, so there is no write-up or write-down: book value stays at par.

questions.q: A \$1000 bond redeems at par with book value \$1038.10 one year before maturity, yield 5%, coupon \$90. Find the final book value at maturity.
questions.explain: Interest $=0.05(1038.10)=51.90$; amortized $=90-51.90=38.10$; $BV=1038.10-38.10=1000.00$ — exactly the par redemption value.

concepts.title: Callable Bonds & Yield to Worst
concepts.tagline: When the issuer can redeem early, price the bond as if the worst call date for you is certain. One rule picks the date.

sections.body: A **callable** bond hands the *issuer* the option to redeem early — and they will exercise it whenever it benefits them, which is exactly when it hurts you. To price safely you must assume the call happens at the worst possible time for the investor. The skill is figuring out, without testing every date, which redemption date is the worst.

sections.title: The issuer calls when it's cheap for them
sections.body: An issuer refinances (calls the bond) when rates have fallen — they would rather reissue cheaply. For *you*, the holder, the price you can safely pay is the **lowest** price across all possible redemption dates, because you must survive the issuer's most unfavorable-to-you choice. So you compute the bond's price at every allowable call date and take the **minimum** — the 'yield to worst' price. Pay more than that and a call could hand you a loss.

sections.title: Premium vs discount decides the call date
sections.body: Compute the price at each candidate redemption date $t$ using the desired yield and take the minimum. A shortcut from the premium/discount sign (level coupons, redemption at par): if the bond is at a **premium** (coupon $>$ yield), the issuer calls **earliest** — price using the *earliest* call date. If at a **discount** (coupon $<$ yield), assume the **latest** date (maturity). Premium → call soon; discount → call late.

sections.title: Pricing a callable premium bond
sections.body: A \$1000 bond pays 9% annual coupons and is callable at par at the end of years 8, 9, or 10. You want a 7% yield. Which date do you price for, and why?
steps: Coupon 9% > yield 7%, so the bond trades at a **premium** at every date.
For a premium bond the price is *lower* the sooner it is called (you lose the remaining above-market coupons earlier).
So the worst case for you is the **earliest** call, end of year 8 — price the bond as a 8-year bond.
Pay no more than that price; if you assumed year 10 you would overpay and a year-8 call would sting.

sections.title: Premium → earliest, discount → latest
sections.body: Memorize the one-liner: **premium bonds get called early, discount bonds run to maturity.** A premium bond loses value as it approaches par, so the issuer redeems it as soon as allowed; price for the earliest call. A discount bond gains value toward par, so the issuer has no reason to call early; price for the latest date. This skips computing every date's price.

sections.title: Call premiums and 'worst for the investor'
sections.body: Two subtleties: (1) if the bond can be called *above* par (a call premium), the redemption value $C$ differs by date, and the simple premium/discount rule may not directly apply — you must price each date explicitly. (2) Always frame it as worst-for-the-**investor** (lowest price), not best-for-the-issuer phrased loosely — they coincide here, but stating it as the minimum price keeps you from inverting the logic under pressure.

cards.front: How do you price a callable bond safely?
cards.back: Compute the price at every allowable redemption date and take the minimum (yield to worst).

cards.front: Premium bond — which call date?
cards.back: Earliest: a premium bond is called as soon as possible.

cards.front: Discount bond — which call date?
cards.back: Latest (maturity): the issuer has no incentive to call early.

cards.front: When does the simple rule break?
cards.back: When the call/redemption value varies by date (call premium) — price each date explicitly.

questions.q: A bond with coupon rate above its yield (a premium bond) callable at par should be priced assuming a call at the:
questions.explain: Premium bonds lose value toward par, so the issuer calls as early as allowed; price for the earliest call.

questions.q: A discount bond (coupon below yield) callable at par should be priced assuming redemption at the:
questions.explain: A discount bond gains value toward par; the issuer won't call early, so use the latest date.

questions.q: The price you should pay for a callable bond is the ____ across all redemption dates.
questions.explain: To be safe against the issuer's worst-for-you choice, pay the minimum price (yield to worst).

questions.q: Why does an issuer call a bond when interest rates fall?
choices: To refinance at a lower rate
questions.explain: Lower market rates let the issuer reissue debt more cheaply, so calling and refinancing benefits them.

questions.q: A bond is callable at par at years 5–10 and is priced to yield less than its coupon. The investor should assume a call at year:
questions.explain: Coupon > yield means a premium bond → called at the earliest date, year 5.

modules.title: Cash Flows, Duration & Immunization
modules.blurb: Yield rates and the general equation of value, plus the interest-rate-risk toolkit: Macaulay and modified duration, convexity, and Redington immunization that protects a portfolio against rate moves.

concepts.title: Yield Rates, NPV & IRR
concepts.tagline: The yield rate is the discount rate that makes a project break even. NPV ranks projects; IRR is the rate where NPV hits zero.

sections.body: Every investment decision comes down to two numbers. **Net present value** asks: at my required rate, is this project worth more than it costs? **Internal rate of return** asks: what rate would make it exactly break even? Together they are how actuaries and analysts rank competing cash-flow streams — and the exam tests both, plus the traps that make IRR misbehave.

sections.title: NPV is value created; IRR is the break-even rate
sections.body: Discount every cash flow — outflows negative, inflows positive — back to today and add them up: that sum is the **NPV** at your chosen rate. Positive means the project earns more than your hurdle rate; you accept it. The **IRR** is the special discount rate at which the NPV is exactly zero — the project's own internal earning rate. Compare it to your required return: if IRR exceeds the hurdle, the project clears the bar.

sections.title: NPV and the IRR condition
sections.body: $$\text{NPV}(i) = \sum_{t} \frac{CF_t}{(1+i)^t}$$ Accept if NPV $> 0$ at the required rate. The **IRR** is the rate $i^*$ solving $$\text{NPV}(i^*) = \sum_t \frac{CF_t}{(1+i^*)^t} = 0$$ For ranking mutually exclusive projects, NPV at the cost of capital is the reliable criterion — IRR can mislead.

sections.title: NPV of a simple project
sections.body: A project costs \$1000 now and returns \$600 at year 1 and \$600 at year 2. At a required rate of 10%, find the NPV and decide.
steps: NPV $> 0$, so the project earns more than 10% — accept it.
(Its IRR is the rate where these balance, a bit above 13%.)

sections.title: NPV beats IRR for ranking
sections.body: When choosing among mutually exclusive projects, rank by **NPV at the cost of capital**, not by IRR. IRR ignores scale (a tiny project can have a huge IRR but create little value) and can give multiple or no answers when cash flows change sign more than once. NPV always gives one clear, value-based ranking. Reach for IRR only when a single break-even rate is what's asked.

sections.title: Multiple IRRs and the reinvestment assumption
sections.body: If the cash-flow signs flip more than once (out, in, out again), Descartes' rule warns there may be **multiple IRRs** — or none — and the single-rate interpretation collapses. Also, IRR implicitly assumes interim cash flows are reinvested *at the IRR itself*, which is often unrealistic; NPV assumes reinvestment at the cost of capital. Quoting a 40% IRR as if you can redeploy cash at 40% is the classic overstatement.

cards.front: What is NPV?
cards.back: The sum of all signed cash flows discounted at the required rate; accept if positive.

cards.front: What is the IRR?
cards.back: The discount rate that makes NPV equal zero — the project's break-even rate.

cards.front: Which criterion ranks mutually exclusive projects?
cards.back: NPV at the cost of capital — IRR can mislead on scale and sign changes.

cards.front: When can multiple IRRs occur?
cards.back: When the cash-flow signs change more than once.

questions.q: A project costs \$500 and returns \$300 at year 1 and \$300 at year 2. At 8%, find the NPV.
The internal rate of return is defined as the rate at which:
questions.explain: IRR is the discount rate making the net present value exactly zero.

questions.q: A project has NPV $> 0$ at your required rate. This means the IRR is:
questions.explain: If NPV is positive at the hurdle rate, the break-even rate (IRR) lies above it.

questions.q: Cash flows are $-100, +260, -165$. Descartes' rule of signs suggests up to how many positive IRRs?
questions.explain: Two sign changes ($-$ to $+$ to $-$) allow up to two positive real IRRs.

questions.q: For ranking two mutually exclusive projects, the preferred criterion is:
choices: Higher NPV at the cost of capital
questions.explain: NPV at the cost of capital ranks by value created and avoids IRR's scale and multiple-root issues.

concepts.title: Dollar-Weighted vs Time-Weighted Yield
concepts.tagline: Two ways to measure a fund's return. One judges the timing of deposits; the other judges the manager. The exam wants both.

sections.body: A fund earns a return — but *whose* return? If a big deposit landed right before a great quarter, was that skill or luck? **Dollar-weighted** yield rewards (or blames) the timing and size of cash flows; **time-weighted** yield strips timing out to isolate the manager's performance. Knowing which to compute, and why they differ, is a guaranteed exam question.

sections.title: Whose decision are you measuring?
sections.body: The **dollar-weighted** return is just the IRR of the fund's actual cash flows — it is heavily influenced by *when* money was added or withdrawn, because more dollars present during good periods lift the result. That measures the *investor's* timing. The **time-weighted** return chains together the growth factor of each sub-period between cash flows, so the size and timing of deposits cancel out — it measures the *manager's* skill, the return on a single dollar left untouched.

sections.title: Both yields
sections.body: **Dollar-weighted (IRR):** solve for $i$ in the equation of value $$A + \sum C_t (1+i)^{1-t} = B$$ where $A$ is the start balance, $B$ the end balance, and $C_t$ the deposits/withdrawals. A common simple approximation: $i \approx \frac{I}{A + \sum C_t(1-t)}$. **Time-weighted:** chain the period factors $$1 + i_{tw} = \prod_k \frac{B_k}{B_{k-1}^{+}}$$ multiplying each sub-period's growth (balance before the next deposit over balance just after the last).

sections.title: Time-weighted return with a mid-year deposit
sections.body: A fund starts at \$100. After 6 months it is worth \$110; you then deposit \$50 (balance \$160). At year-end it is worth \$180. Find the time-weighted yield.
steps: Second sub-period factor: $180/160 = 1.125$ (deposit excluded from the return — it raised the base, not the performance).

sections.title: Deposit before a gain → dollar-weighted is higher
sections.body: Use the relationship as a sanity check: if large deposits arrive *just before* strong performance, the **dollar-weighted** return exceeds the time-weighted one (more money was present to enjoy the gain). If big money arrives before a *poor* stretch, dollar-weighted is lower. Time-weighted is indifferent to all of this — so comparing the two tells you whether the investor's timing helped or hurt.

sections.title: Don't let deposits inflate the time-weighted return
sections.body: The signature error: counting a deposit as investment *gain*. In the worked example, the balance jumped from 110 to 160, but \$50 of that was new money — the performance factor uses $180/160$, not $180/110$. Time-weighting deliberately quarantines cash flows at sub-period boundaries. For dollar-weighting, remember it is an IRR, so a withdrawal is a *negative* cash flow in the equation of value.

cards.front: What is the dollar-weighted yield?
cards.back: The IRR of the fund's actual cash flows — sensitive to deposit timing and size (measures the investor).

cards.front: What is the time-weighted yield?
cards.back: The product of each sub-period's growth factor — removes cash-flow timing (measures the manager).

cards.front: When does dollar-weighted exceed time-weighted?
cards.back: When large deposits arrive just before strong performance.

cards.front: How are deposits handled in time-weighting?
cards.back: Excluded from the return: split sub-periods at each cash flow and use the post-deposit balance as the next base.

questions.q: A fund grows \$100 → \$120 in H1, takes a \$30 deposit (to \$150), then ends H2 at \$165. Find the time-weighted yield.
The dollar-weighted yield is computed as the:
questions.explain: Dollar-weighted return is the internal rate of return solving the fund's equation of value.

questions.q: An investor adds a large sum just before a strong period. Compared to time-weighted, the dollar-weighted return is:
questions.explain: More dollars present during the gain raises the dollar-weighted (IRR) return above the time-weighted figure.

questions.q: Which return best isolates an investment manager's skill, independent of client deposits?
questions.explain: Time-weighting removes the effect of cash-flow timing, leaving the manager's per-dollar performance.

questions.q: Fund: \$1000 start, \$80 interest earned over the year, a \$200 deposit at mid-year. Approximate the dollar-weighted yield via $I/(A+C(1-t))$.

concepts.title: Spot Rates & Forward Rates
concepts.tagline: The yield curve is not one rate but a term structure. Spot rates price each maturity; forward rates are the future rates locked in today.

sections.body: A single interest rate is a convenient fiction. In reality, money for 1 year and money for 5 years command *different* rates — the **term structure**. **Spot rates** are today's rate for each maturity; **forward rates** are the rates for future periods that today's curve implicitly locks in. Reading one off the other is a high-frequency FM skill, and it powers swaps and bond pricing alike.

sections.title: No-arbitrage links the long path to the short paths
sections.body: Investing for 2 years at the 2-year spot rate must give the *same* growth as investing 1 year at the 1-year spot and then rolling into a rate locked in today for year 2 — otherwise a riskless profit exists. That locked-in second-year rate is the **forward rate**. So the long spot rate is a geometric blend of the short spot and the forwards: the multi-year accumulation factors must agree no matter how you slice the path.

sections.title: Spot–forward relationship
sections.body: Let $s_t$ be the $t$-year spot rate and $f_{[t-1,t]}$ the 1-year forward covering year $t$. No-arbitrage requires: $$(1+s_t)^t = (1+s_{t-1})^{t-1}\,(1+f_{[t-1,t]})$$ so the forward is $$f_{[t-1,t]} = \frac{(1+s_t)^t}{(1+s_{t-1})^{t-1}} - 1$$ A cash flow at time $t$ is priced with its own spot: $PV = \frac{CF_t}{(1+s_t)^t}$.

widget.caption: Drag the spot rates $s_1,\dots,s_4$ and watch the implied 1-year forward rates update via $(1+s_t)^t=(1+s_{t-1})^{t-1}(1+f)$. An upward-sloping spot curve forces forwards *above* the spots; an inverted curve pushes them below — the forwards always 'lever' the curve's slope.

sections.title: Forward rate from two spot rates
sections.body: The 1-year spot rate is 4% and the 2-year spot rate is 5%. Find the 1-year forward rate for year 2.
steps: Note the forward (6%) sits *above* both spots — the upward curve forces year 2's marginal rate higher than the average.

sections.title: Forwards exaggerate the curve's slope
sections.body: A reliable intuition: when the spot curve **rises**, each forward rate lies *above* the spot for that maturity; when it **falls** (inverted), forwards lie *below*. The forward is the marginal rate for one specific future year, so it must overshoot the cumulative average that the spot represents. If your computed forward sits between two rising spots, you made an arithmetic error.

sections.title: Discount each cash flow at its own spot rate
sections.body: The biggest term-structure error is discounting *all* cash flows at a single yield. With a term structure, a payment at time $t$ must be discounted at the **$t$-year spot rate** $s_t$, not at $s_1$ or some flat average. Mixing maturities under one rate misprices the bond. Second trap: forward-rate exponents — the $(t-1)$ and $t$ powers must match the spot maturities exactly, or the geometric link breaks.

cards.front: Spot–forward no-arbitrage relation?
How do you price a cash flow under a term structure?
cards.back: Discount each $CF_t$ at its own $t$-year spot rate: $CF_t/(1+s_t)^t$.

cards.front: Rising spot curve — where are forwards?
cards.back: Above the spot rates (forwards exaggerate the slope).

cards.front: What is a forward rate?
cards.back: The interest rate for a future period locked in by today's spot curve.

questions.q: 1-year spot $=3\%$, 2-year spot $=4\%$. Find the 1-year forward rate for year 2.
Under a term structure, a \$1000 cash flow at year 3 with $s_3 = 6\%$ has present value:
questions.explain: Discount at its own 3-year spot rate: $1000/(1.06)^3$.

questions.q: If the spot curve is downward-sloping (inverted), the 1-year forward rates are generally:
questions.explain: A falling curve pushes the marginal forward rates below the spot rates.

questions.q: 2-year spot $=5\%$, and the 1-year forward for year 2 is $7\%$. Find the 1-year spot rate.
The forward rate $f_{[t-1,t]}$ represents:
choices: A future 1-year rate locked in today
questions.explain: It is the rate for the single future year $t$, implied (locked in) by today's spot curve.

concepts.title: Interest Rate Swaps
concepts.tagline: Trade a floating-rate obligation for a fixed one. The swap rate is the level fixed rate with the same present value as the expected floating payments.

sections.body: A company with a floating-rate loan hates uncertainty; another with a fixed loan wants to bet on falling rates. An **interest rate swap** lets them trade payment streams: one pays fixed, receives floating; the other does the reverse. No principal changes hands — only the interest difference. The exam asks you to find the fair **swap rate** and value an existing swap, both of which reduce to the spot curve you already know.

sections.title: A swap is a portfolio of forward rate agreements
sections.body: Each period of a swap exchanges a fixed payment for that period's floating rate — which, priced today, is the **forward rate**. So a swap is really a bundle of forward-rate agreements stacked across the term. The fair fixed rate (the **swap rate**) is the single level rate whose payments have the *same present value* as the whole strip of forward (floating) payments. Set the two legs' PVs equal and solve for the fixed rate.

sections.title: The swap rate
sections.body: Using spot rates $s_t$ and discount factors $P(0,t) = (1+s_t)^{-t}$, the level swap rate $R$ on notional 1 for $n$ years satisfies (fixed leg PV = floating leg PV): $$R = \frac{1 - P(0,n)}{\sum_{t=1}^{n} P(0,t)} = \frac{1 - (1+s_n)^{-n}}{\sum_{t=1}^n (1+s_t)^{-t}}$$ The numerator is the floating leg's value; the denominator is the annuity of discount factors.

sections.title: A two-year swap rate
sections.body: Spot rates are $s_1 = 4\%$ and $s_2 = 5\%$. Find the fixed swap rate on a 2-year swap.

sections.title: Swap rate is a discount-factor-weighted average of forwards
sections.body: The swap rate always lands *between* the spot/forward rates across the term — it is essentially their present-value-weighted average. So a quick sanity check: a 2-year swap rate must sit between $s_1$ and $s_2$. If your answer falls outside that range, you inverted a discount factor. The numerator $1 - P(0,n)$ is also exactly the value of receiving all the floating payments — memorize that shortcut.

sections.title: Notional is not exchanged; net the payments
sections.body: Two recurring traps: (1) the **notional principal never changes hands** — only the *difference* between fixed and floating interest is settled each period, so don't add principal to either leg's cash flows. (2) To **value** an existing swap mid-life (not just find its initial rate), recompute both legs at the *current* spot curve; a swap is worth zero only at inception, then drifts as rates move.

cards.front: What is an interest rate swap?
cards.back: An exchange of fixed-rate for floating-rate interest payments on a notional, with no principal exchanged.

cards.front: Swap rate formula?
Why is a swap a strip of FRAs?
cards.back: Each period swaps fixed for that period's forward (floating) rate.

cards.front: Value of a swap at inception?
cards.back: Zero — the fixed and floating legs have equal present value by construction.

questions.q: In a plain vanilla interest rate swap, what is exchanged each period?
questions.explain: Only the difference between the fixed and floating interest on the notional is settled; principal is never exchanged.

questions.q: Discount factors are $P(0,1)=0.95$ and $P(0,2)=0.89$. Find the 2-year swap rate.
The value of a newly initiated (fair) interest rate swap is:
questions.explain: By construction the swap rate equates the two legs' present values, so the swap is worth zero at inception.

questions.q: A 3-year swap has spot rates 3%, 4%, 5%. The swap rate must lie:
questions.explain: The swap rate is a discount-factor-weighted average of the term structure, so it falls within the spot range.

questions.q: To value an existing swap two years into its life, you should:
choices: Use the original swap rate's discount factors
Recompute both legs at the current spot curve
Assume it is still worth zero
Add the notional to the fixed leg
questions.explain: A swap is zero-value only at inception; afterward revalue both legs at the prevailing spot rates.

concepts.title: Duration & Immunization
concepts.tagline: Duration is how rate-sensitive a cash flow is. Immunization is matching that sensitivity so a rate move can't hurt you.

sections.body: When interest rates move, the value of every future cash flow moves with them. **Duration** measures exactly how much, and **immunization** is the art of arranging assets so that a rate shock leaves your surplus untouched. This is the conceptual peak of FM — and a favorite of the exam writers.

sections.title: Duration is the cash flow's center of gravity in time
sections.body: Picture each payment as a weight placed on a timeline, the weight being its present value. **Macaulay duration** is the balance point of those weights — the average time, PV-weighted, at which you get paid. Longer duration means cash arrives later, which means *more* sensitivity to rate changes. **Modified duration** then converts that into the percentage price drop per 1% rate rise.

sections.title: Duration and convexity
sections.body: Macaulay duration: $$D_{mac} = \frac{\sum t\, v^t\, CF_t}{\sum v^t\, CF_t} = \frac{\sum t\,\cdot PV_t}{P}$$ Modified duration: $D_{mod} = \dfrac{D_{mac}}{1+i}$. First-order price change: $$\frac{\Delta P}{P} \approx -D_{mod}\,\Delta i$$ Convexity adds the second-order correction $+\tfrac12 C(\Delta i)^2$.

sections.title: Duration of a two-payment stream
sections.body: Cash flows of \$100 at year 1 and \$100 at year 2, at $i = 10\%$. Find the Macaulay duration.

sections.title: Estimate price moves with one multiplication
sections.body: Once you have modified duration, a rate change's price impact is a single product: $\Delta P/P \approx -D_{mod}\,\Delta i$. A bond with $D_{mod} = 7$ loses about 7% if rates rise 1%. This linear estimate is exam-fast; convexity only matters when they ask for a refined answer on a large rate move.

sections.title: Forgetting the Redington conditions
sections.body: Immunization is not just matching present values. **Redington immunization** needs three conditions: (1) asset PV = liability PV, (2) asset duration = liability duration, and (3) asset convexity > liability convexity. Skip the convexity condition and your 'immunized' portfolio still loses to large rate moves. All three must hold.

cards.front: What does Macaulay duration represent?
cards.back: The PV-weighted average time until cash flows are received — the timeline's center of gravity.

cards.front: Relationship between modified and Macaulay duration?
The three Redington immunization conditions?
cards.back: PV of assets = PV of liabilities; durations equal; asset convexity > liability convexity.

questions.q: A zero-coupon bond pays \$1000 in 7 years. What is its Macaulay duration?
questions.explain: A single payment's PV-weighted average time is just its own maturity: 7 years. A zero-coupon bond's Macaulay duration equals its time to maturity.

questions.q: A bond has modified duration 6. If interest rates rise by 0.5%, the approximate percentage price change is:
questions.explain: $\Delta P/P \approx -D_{mod}\,\Delta i = -6(0.005) = -0.03 = -3\%$.

questions.q: If Macaulay duration is 8.4 years and $i = 5\%$, find the modified duration.
Which is NOT a required condition for Redington immunization?
choices: PV of assets equals PV of liabilities
Duration of assets equals duration of liabilities
Convexity of assets exceeds convexity of liabilities
Asset cash flows occur before liability cash flows
All three standard conditions hold simultaneously
questions.explain: Redington requires equal PVs, equal durations, and greater asset convexity. There is no requirement that asset cash flows precede liabilities — that describes exact (dedicated) matching, not Redington immunization.

questions.q: Two equal-PV cash flow streams have durations 4 and 9 years. To immunize a liability of duration 6 using both, the weight on the 4-year stream is closest to:
questions.explain: Solve $4w + 9(1-w) = 6 \Rightarrow 9 - 5w = 6 \Rightarrow 5w = 3 \Rightarrow w = 0.6 = 60\%$.

concepts.title: Convexity & Cash-Flow Matching
concepts.tagline: Duration is the straight-line estimate; convexity is the curve it misses. Exact matching sidesteps both by funding each liability directly.

sections.body: Duration assumes the price-rate relationship is a straight line — but it is actually a **curve**, bowed toward the origin. **Convexity** measures that curvature, and it is always your friend: it makes bonds gain a little more when rates fall and lose a little less when they rise. The exam tests convexity as a second-order correction and contrasts immunization with its airtight cousin, **exact cash-flow matching**.

sections.title: The price curve bows above the duration line
sections.body: Plot bond price against interest rate: it slopes down (higher rates, lower price) but **curves upward** — convex. Duration is the tangent line at today's rate, a decent estimate for small moves but it underestimates the price for *any* move, up or down, because the true curve lies above the tangent. Convexity quantifies that gap. More convexity means more cushion against large rate swings — a desirable, free-ish property.

sections.title: Second-order price change and matching
sections.body: The Taylor expansion of price in the rate adds a convexity term: $$\frac{\Delta P}{P} \approx -D_{mod}\,\Delta i + \tfrac{1}{2}\,C\,(\Delta i)^2$$ where convexity $C = \frac{1}{P}\frac{d^2P}{di^2} = \frac{\sum t(t+1)\,v^{t+2} CF_t}{P}$ (one common form). **Exact (dedicated) matching:** choose assets whose cash flows *equal* each liability at every date — then no rate move matters at all, no duration or convexity needed.

sections.title: Convexity-adjusted price change
sections.body: A bond has modified duration 8 and convexity 120. Rates rise by 2% ($\Delta i = 0.02$). Estimate the percentage price change with and without the convexity correction.
steps: Convexity softens the loss — the true drop is smaller than duration alone predicts.

sections.title: Convexity always helps the holder
sections.body: The convexity term is $+\tfrac12 C(\Delta i)^2$ — and since $(\Delta i)^2 \ge 0$ and $C > 0$ for ordinary bonds, it is **always positive**, whether rates rise or fall. So for two bonds with equal duration, the more convex one is strictly preferable: it falls less and rises more. This is exactly why Redington immunization demands asset convexity *greater* than liability convexity — the surplus stays non-negative for moves in either direction.

sections.title: Matching vs immunization are different guarantees
sections.body: Don't conflate the two strategies. **Exact matching** funds each liability with an asset cash flow of the same amount and date — perfect protection, but often impractical or expensive. **Immunization** (Redington) only matches PV, duration, and convexity, protecting against *small* parallel rate shifts; it can still fail under large or non-parallel moves. Matching needs no rebalancing; immunization must be **rebalanced** as time passes and rates move, since durations drift.

cards.front: What does convexity measure?
cards.back: The curvature of the price-rate relationship — the second-order term duration misses.

cards.front: Sign of the convexity price adjustment?
cards.back: Always positive ($+\tfrac12 C(\Delta i)^2$): it helps the holder either way rates move.

cards.front: Exact (dedicated) cash-flow matching?
cards.back: Assets whose cash flows equal each liability at every date — immune to any rate move, no rebalancing.

cards.front: Why must immunization be rebalanced?
cards.back: Durations and PVs drift with time and rate changes, so the match degrades and must be reset.

questions.q: A bond has modified duration 5 and convexity 80. For $\Delta i = +0.01$, the convexity correction to $\Delta P/P$ is:
The convexity adjustment to a bond's price change is:
questions.explain: $\tfrac12 C(\Delta i)^2 \ge 0$ for ordinary bonds regardless of the direction of the rate move.

questions.q: Two bonds have equal duration. The one with higher convexity will:
choices: Outperform for large rate moves either way
questions.explain: Greater convexity means it falls less and rises more, so it outperforms when rates move substantially in either direction.

questions.q: Which strategy provides protection without any need to rebalance over time?
questions.explain: Exact (dedicated) matching funds each liability directly, so it needs no rebalancing and is immune to any rate change.

questions.q: Compared to the duration-only estimate, including positive convexity makes the predicted price for a rate increase:
questions.explain: The positive convexity term offsets part of the duration loss, raising the predicted price (a smaller drop).

concepts.title: Determinants of Interest Rates
concepts.tagline: Where rates come from: a real return, an inflation premium, and compensation for default, liquidity, and maturity risk. The qualitative capstone.

sections.body: Every rate you have discounted with on this exam is built from parts. A lender demands a **real** return for deferring consumption, plus compensation for **inflation**, plus premiums for the chance of **default**, for tying money up (**liquidity**), and for the **term** of the loan. Understanding this decomposition is the qualitative capstone of FM — and the SOA tests it directly.

sections.title: Stack the compensations a lender requires
sections.body: Start with the **real risk-free rate** — what you'd earn with no inflation and no risk, purely for waiting. Add an **inflation premium** so your repayment keeps its purchasing power. Then layer risk premiums: a **default (credit)** premium for the borrower possibly not paying, a **liquidity** premium if the asset is hard to sell, and a **maturity/term** premium for longer commitments. The quoted nominal rate is the sum of all these demands.

sections.title: Fisher equation and the rate stack
sections.body: The **Fisher equation** links nominal $i$, real $r$, and inflation $\pi$: $$(1+i) = (1+r)(1+\pi) \;\approx\; i \approx r + \pi$$ The full nominal rate is approximately $$i \approx r + \pi + (\text{default}) + (\text{liquidity}) + (\text{maturity premium})$$ Real rate exactly: $1 + r = \frac{1+i}{1+\pi}$.

sections.title: Real rate via the Fisher equation
sections.body: A bond yields a nominal 8% while inflation runs 3%. Find the exact real rate of return.
steps: The quick approximation $r \approx i - \pi = 8\% - 3\% = 5\%$ is close but slightly overstates it.
The gap (5% vs 4.85%) is the cross-term $r\pi$ the approximation drops.

sections.title: Approximate, then refine with Fisher
sections.body: For a fast estimate use $r \approx i - \pi$; it is within a few basis points for ordinary rates. When precision matters, switch to the exact $1+r = \frac{1+i}{1+\pi}$, which always gives a *slightly lower* real rate than the subtraction (the dropped $r\pi$ term is positive). Knowing the direction of the error lets you sanity-check multiple-choice answers instantly.

sections.title: Real vs nominal, and which premium is which
sections.body: Keep the layers straight: a **higher inflation** expectation raises the *nominal* rate but not the real rate; a **riskier borrower** raises the *default* premium; an illiquid asset raises the *liquidity* premium. Confusing inflation compensation with a risk premium is the classic conceptual slip. And don't subtract inflation twice — the nominal rate already includes it, so the *real* return is what's left after removing it once.

cards.front: Components of a nominal interest rate?
cards.back: Real rate + inflation premium + default + liquidity + maturity/term premiums.

cards.front: Fisher equation?
cards.back: $(1+i) = (1+r)(1+\pi)$; approximately $i \approx r + \pi$.

cards.front: Exact real rate from nominal and inflation?
cards.back: $1+r = \frac{1+i}{1+\pi}$ — slightly below $i-\pi$.

cards.front: What does a default premium compensate for?
cards.back: The risk the borrower fails to repay (credit risk).

questions.q: Nominal rate 10%, inflation 4%. Find the exact real rate.
questions.explain: $1+r = 1.10/1.04 = 1.05769$, so $r \approx 5.77\%$ — just under the $6\%$ approximation.

questions.q: Which premium compensates a lender for the risk that the borrower may not repay?
questions.explain: The default or credit risk premium covers the chance of non-repayment.

questions.q: By the Fisher equation, the approximation $i \approx r + \pi$ omits which term?
questions.explain: $(1+r)(1+\pi) = 1 + r + \pi + r\pi$; the approximation drops the cross-term $r\pi$.

questions.q: All else equal, an increase in expected inflation primarily raises the:
questions.explain: Inflation expectations are passed into the nominal rate, leaving the real rate roughly unchanged.

questions.q: An asset that is difficult to sell quickly without a price concession commands a higher:
questions.explain: Hard-to-trade assets carry a liquidity premium to compensate holders for that difficulty.
